raw_text:
### Introduction and Pathophysiology

Heart failure (HF) remains a major global public health challenge, characterized by high rates of morbidity, hospitalization, and mortality. Pathophysiologically, HF is driven by chronic neurohormonal activation, primarily involving the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and the sympathetic nervous system. In contrast, the counter-regulatory natriuretic peptide (NP) system promotes vasodilation, natriuresis, and diuresis, while inhibiting cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis. Dual neurohormonal modulation—suppressing the harmful effects of the RAAS while enhancing the beneficial effects of the NP system—became a primary therapeutic target. Early attempts at dual inhibition paired an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor with a neprilysin inhibitor (e.g., omapatrilat in the OVERTURE trial); however, this combination led to an unacceptable risk of life-threatening angioedema due to simultaneous inhibition of three major bradykinin clearance pathways [1].

To overcome this safety barrier, sacubitril/valsartan (originally LCZ696) was developed as a first-in-class angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) [2]. By combining the neprilysin inhibitor prodrug sacubitril with the angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) valsartan, sacubitril/valsartan successfully modulates both pathways while minimizing angioedema risk [2,3].

### Clinical Efficacy in HFrEF

In patients with HF and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), the landmark PARADIGM-HF trial demonstrated the profound clinical efficacy of sacubitril/valsartan [4]. Comparing ARNI to the ACE inhibitor enalapril in 8,399 patients, sacubitril/valsartan achieved a 20% relative risk reduction in the primary composite outcome of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization [4]. Sub-studies of PARADIGM-HF revealed consistent therapeutic benefits across all age groups [5], a significant reduction in both sudden cardiac death and death due to worsening heart failure [6], and fewer recurrent clinical events [7]. Furthermore, sacubitril/valsartan therapy was associated with a notable decrease in the necessity for loop diuretic intensification, reflecting a reduction in outpatient clinical worsening [8]. In addition to prognostic benefits, sacubitril/valsartan led to sustained improvements in health-related quality of life [9]. From a safety perspective, while symptomatic hypotension was more frequent in the ARNI group, it did not increase treatment discontinuations [10].

Beyond clinical endpoints, the mechanistic underpinnings of ARNI's superiority were demonstrated through cardiac reverse remodeling. The open-label PROVE-HF trial showed that sacubitril/valsartan initiation was strongly associated with significant reductions in N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) that correlated with improvements in left ventricular volume and ejection fraction [11]. Simultaneously, the randomized EVALUATE-HF trial demonstrated favorable effects on aortic stiffness and cardiac volumes compared to enalapril [12].

### In-Hospital Initiation and Acute Heart Failure

Transitioning to the acute setting, the PIONEER-HF trial established the safety and efficacy of initiating sacubitril/valsartan in patients hospitalized with acute decompensated HF once hemodynamically stabilized, showing a more rapid reduction in NT-proBNP than enalapril [13], which translated to reduced post-discharge clinical events at 8 weeks [14]. This approach was supported by the TRANSITION trial, which demonstrated that pre-discharge initiation of sacubitril/valsartan was highly feasible and well-tolerated [15].

### Efficacy in HFpEF and HFmrEF

Historically, therapeutic options for HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF) were sparse. The phase II PARAMOUNT trial first showed that sacubitril/valsartan significantly reduced NT-proBNP and left atrial volume compared to valsartan in HFpEF [3]. This led to the phase III PARAGON-HF trial in patients with an ejection fraction ≥45% [16]. Although sacubitril/valsartan did not achieve statistical significance for the overall primary endpoint of total HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular death [16], prespecified subgroup analyses and subsequent pooled analyses across the ejection fraction spectrum [17], including a putative placebo analysis [18], suggested clinical benefits extending into the mildly reduced range (LVEF up to ~57–60%), particularly in women. This was further illuminated by the PARAGLIDE-HF trial, which demonstrated that ARNI reduced NT-proBNP and worsening HF events in patients with LVEF >40% stabilized after an acute event [19]. Prespecified participant-level pooled analyses of PARAGON-HF and PARAGLIDE-HF confirmed robust reductions in cardiovascular and renal events in this population [20].

### Special Populations, Comorbidities, and Safety

The benefits of sacubitril/valsartan extend to key comorbidities. In patients with HFrEF and type 2 diabetes, ARNI improved glycemic control [21] and slowed the rate of decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) compared to enalapril [22]. In chronic kidney disease (CKD) without heart failure, the UK HARP-III trial demonstrated renal safety comparable to irbesartan alongside a reduction in cardiac biomarkers [23]. 

However, sacubitril/valsartan does not benefit all HF phenotypes equally. In high-risk survivors of acute myocardial infarction (AMI), the PARADISE-MI trial did not demonstrate a significant reduction in cardiovascular death or incident HF compared to ramipril [24]. Similarly, in patients with advanced HFrEF (NYHA class IV), the LIFE trial showed no significant difference in clinical outcomes or NT-proBNP reduction between sacubitril/valsartan and valsartan [25]. Conversely, pediatric heart failure remains a successful frontier; the PANORAMA-HF trial confirmed the pharmacokinetic, safety, and biomarker efficacy profiles of sacubitril/valsartan in children [26].

Despite robust clinical trial data, real-world translation remains a challenge. Data from the CHAMP-HF registry showed low rates of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) up-titration and highlighted marked heterogeneity in treatment patterns [27].

### Guideline Recommendations and Conclusion

Based on this collective body of evidence, international clinical guidelines have been revolutionized. The 2021 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines [28] and their 2023 Focused Update [29], alongside the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guidelines [30], designate sacubitril/valsartan with a Class I recommendation as a foundational pillar of GDMT in patients with HFrEF, and recommend it (Class IIa/IIb) in those with HFmrEF and HFpEF. Sacubitril/valsartan represents a critical milestone in cardiovascular medicine, transitioning treatment from pure neurohormonal inhibition to active neurohormonal modulation.
